# Introduction

The study presented here is primarily motivated by a recent experimental measurement of the branching ratio for the decay $B_d^0 \to J/\psi \eta$. This new experimental result provides an important opportunity to confront theoretical predictions with data and to test our understanding of the underlying dynamics governing this class of $B$ meson decays.

In order to provide a theoretical benchmark and to interpret the experimental measurement within the framework of the Standard Model, we calculate the branching ratios of both $B_d^0 \to J/\psi \eta$ and $B_d^0 \to J/\psi \eta'$ decays using the perturbative QCD (pQCD) approach. This approach allows for a systematic treatment of the strong interaction dynamics involved in these hadronic $B$ meson transitions, incorporating the relevant form factors and decay amplitudes within a consistent theoretical framework.

Our calculation yields a pQCD prediction for the branching ratio of the $\eta$ channel of
$$BR(B_d^0 \to J/\psi \eta) = \left(1.96^{+9.68}_{-0.65}\right) \times 10^{-6},$$
which is found to be in agreement, within the quoted theoretical and experimental uncertainties, with the first experimental measurement of this decay mode. This consistency represents an important validation of the pQCD framework in describing this particular decay channel.

For the analogous decay involving the $\eta'$ meson, our pQCD calculation predicts
$$BR(B_d^0 \to J/\psi \eta') = \left(1.09^{+3.76}_{-0.25}\right) \times 10^{-6}.$$
This branching ratio is found to be similar in magnitude to that of the $\eta$ channel, reflecting the comparable underlying dynamics between the two decay modes. As no experimental measurement currently exists for this channel, this prediction awaits future verification, potentially from forthcoming LHC experiments with increased statistics and improved sensitivity.

Taken together, these two decay channels offer valuable opportunities to advance our understanding of $B$ meson physics. Precise experimental measurements of $B_d^0 \to J/\psi \eta$ and $B_d^0 \to J/\psi \eta'$ decays can help to clarify the nature of QCD dynamics at the energy scale relevant to these processes, particularly concerning the role of $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing and the associated form factors. Furthermore, comparison between theoretical predictions and experimental results serves as a crucial test of the reliability and predictive power of the pQCD approach when applied to this category of $B$ meson decays, thereby contributing to the broader effort of validating theoretical frameworks used in heavy flavor physics.

# Branching Ratios of $B_d^0 \to J/\psi\,\eta^{(\prime)}$ Decays in the Perturbative QCD Approach

## Introduction and Motivation

The study of exclusive hadronic $B$ meson decays involving charmonium states, particularly $J/\psi$, has long served as a powerful laboratory for testing our understanding of both weak and strong interaction dynamics. Decays such as $B_d^0 \to J/\psi K_S^0$ have played a historic role in establishing $CP$ violation in the $B$ meson system and in extracting fundamental parameters of the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) matrix. Building on this foundation, the broader class of $B \to J/\psi + (\text{light meson})$ decays continues to attract theoretical and experimental attention, both as precision tests of the Standard Model and as potential windows into new physics contributions that might manifest through loop-level processes.

Among these decays, the channels $B_d^0 \to J/\psi\,\eta$ and $B_d^0 \to J/\psi\,\eta'$ occupy a special position due to the nontrivial flavor structure of the $\eta$-$\eta'$ system. Unlike simpler pseudoscalar mesons, the physical $\eta$ and $\eta'$ states arise from the mixing of the SU(3) flavor octet and singlet states, with the singlet component receiving additional contributions from the QCD axial anomaly through gluonic and possibly $c\bar{c}$ admixtures. This makes these decay channels theoretically interesting probes of the underlying quark-flavor content and mixing dynamics of the $\eta$-$\eta'$ system, in addition to providing tests of the weak decay mechanism itself.

Until recently, experimental data on $B_d^0 \to J/\psi\,\eta^{(\prime)}$ decays were scarce, limiting the ability to confront theoretical predictions with measurement. However, a recent experimental measurement of the branching ratio for $B_d^0 \to J/\psi\,\eta$ has renewed interest in performing a careful and systematic theoretical calculation of both this channel and its close relative $B_d^0 \to J/\psi\,\eta'$. Such a calculation is timely, as it allows for a direct comparison with the new experimental result and provides a foundation for anticipated future measurements at the LHC, where increased statistics from LHCb and other detectors will substantially improve the precision of branching ratio determinations for these and related decay modes.

## Theoretical Framework: The pQCD Approach

In this work, the authors employ the perturbative QCD (pQCD) approach, based on $k_T$ factorization, to calculate the branching ratios of the $B_d^0 \to J/\psi\,\eta$ and $B_d^0 \to J/\psi\,\eta'$ decays. The pQCD framework has been widely and successfully applied to a large number of exclusive $B$ meson decay channels, offering a systematic method for computing decay amplitudes that incorporates both the perturbative hard-scattering kernels and the nonperturbative meson wave functions.

A key advantage of the $k_T$ factorization scheme underlying the pQCD approach is its ability to regulate the endpoint singularities that plague collinear factorization approaches (such as QCD factorization) when applied to certain decay topologies, including annihilation-type diagrams. By retaining the transverse momentum of the quarks inside the mesons, the pQCD framework naturally introduces a Sudakov factor that suppresses long-distance contributions and stabilizes the endpoint region, thereby allowing a consistent perturbative calculation of the relevant decay amplitudes, including both the emission and annihilation-type contributions that can be relevant for these color-suppressed decay channels.

For the specific decays under consideration, the calculation requires careful treatment of several theoretical ingredients: the $B$ meson wave function, the light-cone distribution amplitudes of the $\eta$ and $\eta'$ mesons (incorporating the appropriate mixing scheme, such as the quark-flavor basis mixing angle), and the nonrelativistic treatment of the $c\bar{c}$ pair forming the $J/\psi$ meson. The interplay between the perturbative hard kernel, computed at leading order in $\alpha_s$, and these nonperturbative inputs allows for a first-principles-based estimate of the decay amplitudes, with theoretical uncertainties arising primarily from the choice of input parameters such as the $B$ meson decay constant, the shape parameters of the wave functions, and the CKM matrix elements.

## Results

Using this framework, the authors obtain the following pQCD predictions for the branching ratios:

$$BR(B_d^0 \to J/\psi\,\eta) = \left(1.96^{+9.68}_{-0.65}\right) \times 10^{-6}$$

$$BR(B_d^0 \to J/\psi\,\eta') = \left(1.09^{+3.76}_{-0.25}\right) \times 10^{-6}$$

The quoted uncertainties reflect the combined effect of varying the relevant input parameters within their allowed ranges, including the hard scale choices, the shape parameters of the meson distribution amplitudes, and the CKM matrix elements. The notably asymmetric uncertainties, with large upper errors, primarily stem from the sensitivity of the annihilation-type contributions to the hard scale and endpoint behavior in the pQCD calculation.

Importantly, these theoretical predictions are found to be in good agreement with the existing experimental measurement of the $B_d^0 \to J/\psi\,\eta$ branching ratio, lending support to the validity of the pQCD approach when applied to this class of $B$ meson decays involving charmonium and light pseudoscalar mesons with nontrivial flavor mixing.

## Implications and Outlook

The agreement between the pQCD predictions and the available experimental data for $B_d^0 \to J/\psi\,\eta$ serves as an important validation of the theoretical framework for this class of decays, which involve the interplay of weak decay dynamics, strong-interaction hadronization, and the flavor mixing structure of the $\eta$-$\eta'$ system. Since the pQCD prediction for $B_d^0 \to J/\psi\,\eta'$ has not yet been directly tested against experiment, this result stands as a genuine prediction awaiting confrontation with future data.

Given the anticipated increase in statistics from ongoing and future LHC runs, particularly at LHCb, more precise measurements of both $BR(B_d^0 \to J/\psi\,\eta)$ and $BR(B_d^0 \to J/\psi\,\eta')$ are expected in the near future. Such measurements will provide a stringent test of the pQCD predictions presented here and may further illuminate the role of $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing, including possible contributions from the gluonic or charm-quark content of the $\eta'$ meson, in these decay channels.

More broadly, this study contributes to the ongoing effort to establish the pQCD approach as a reliable and predictive tool for calculating branching ratios and other observables in $B$ meson decays to charmonium and light mesons, complementing similar analyses carried out within QCD factorization and soft-collinear effective theory frameworks. The consistency of these different theoretical approaches, when confronted with increasingly precise experimental data, will play a crucial role in deepening our understanding of QCD dynamics in heavy meson decays and in probing for potential signals of physics beyond the Standard Model in these processes.

# Motivation, Psi, and QCD: Understanding the J/ψ Particle

## Introduction

The discovery of the J/ψ particle in November 1974 stands as one of the most significant events in the history of particle physics—often called the "November Revolution." Understanding why physicists were motivated to search for such particles, what psi (ψ) mesons represent, and how Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) explains their behavior reveals a fascinating chapter in our understanding of fundamental matter.

## The Motivation Behind the Search

By the early 1970s, physicists faced significant theoretical puzzles. The quark model, proposed by Murray Gell-Mann and George Zweig, had successfully organized known hadrons into patterns, but it remained incomplete. Three quark flavors (up, down, strange) were known, yet theoretical considerations—particularly the GIM mechanism proposed by Glashow, Iliopoulos, and Maiani—suggested a fourth quark, called "charm," should exist to explain the suppression of certain rare particle decays.

This theoretical motivation drove two independent experimental teams to search for new particles:
- Samuel Ting's group at Brookhaven National Laboratory
- Burton Richter's group at SLAC

Their simultaneous discovery of the same particle, observed through different production mechanisms, lent extraordinary credibility to the finding.

## What is the Psi (ψ) Particle?

The particle discovered was named J (by Ting's team) and ψ (by Richter's team)—hence its combined designation J/ψ. This particle turned out to be a **meson composed of a charm quark and its antiquark (charm-anticharm, or cc̄)**, making it what physicists call "charmonium."

What made the J/ψ so remarkable was its unusually narrow width and long lifetime compared to other hadrons of similar mass (about 3.1 GeV/c²). This suggested that whatever quarks composed it were somehow "hidden" or suppressed from decaying through the strong force—a puzzle that pointed directly toward new quark physics.

## The QCD Connection

Quantum Chromodynamics, the theory describing the strong nuclear force, provided the framework to understand why J/ψ behaved so unusually:

1. **Confirmation of Charm**: The J/ψ's properties confirmed the existence of the charm quark, validating the four-quark model and strengthening the broader Standard Model framework.

2. **Asymptotic Freedom**: QCD's property of asymptotic freedom—where quarks interact more weakly at short distances—helped explain the narrow decay width of J/ψ. The heavy charm quarks, bound tightly together, decay through a process requiring the annihilation of quark-antiquark pairs into gluons, which is suppressed according to QCD calculations (related to the OZI rule).

3. **Charmonium Spectroscopy**: The discovery opened the door to studying an entire family of charmonium states (ψ', ψ'', χc states, etc.), providing a "hydrogen atom" analog for testing QCD predictions about quark confinement and the strong force potential between quarks.

4. **Validation of the Quark-Gluon Framework**: The success of QCD in explaining charmonium spectra—using potential models analogous to those in atomic physics—demonstrated that quarks and gluons were not merely mathematical conveniences but physical constituents governed by a coherent quantum field theory.

## Conclusion

The story of the J/ψ particle exemplifies how theoretical motivation, guided by anomalies in existing data, can lead to transformative experimental discoveries. The psi particle's discovery not only confirmed the fourth quark flavor but also provided crucial evidence supporting QCD as the correct theory of the strong force. This convergence of theoretical prediction and experimental verification helped cement the Standard Model of particle physics, illustrating the powerful interplay between motivation, discovery, and theoretical understanding that drives progress in fundamental physics.

We report the first measurement of the branching fraction for the decay $B_d^0 \to J/\psi\,\eta$, a channel that has remained experimentally inaccessible until now due to its suppressed rate and the challenging reconstruction of the $\eta$ meson through its neutral decay modes. Using a data sample collected at a $B$-factory/hadron collider experiment, we reconstruct $J/\psi \to \ell^+\ell^-$ ($\ell = e, \mu$) in combination with $\eta \to \gamma\gamma$ and $\eta \to \pi^+\pi^-\pi^0$ decay modes, achieving a signal significance sufficient to establish this decay for the first time. $$\mathcal{B}(B_d^0 \to J/\psi\,\eta) = (X.X \pm X.X_{\text{stat}} \pm X.X_{\text{syst}}) \times 10^{-5},$$

consistent within uncertainties with predictions from perturbative QCD (pQCD) factorization approaches that incorporate next-to-leading-order (NLO) vertex and hard-spectator corrections, as well as $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing effects parametrized in the quark-flavor basis. This measurement provides a critical test of the dynamics governing color-suppressed $b \to c\bar{c}s$ transitions accompanied by $SU(3)$-flavor-singlet contributions from the $\eta$ meson wavefunction, and helps disentangle the relative size of the singlet and non-singlet decay amplitudes.

$$\mathcal{B}(B_d^0 \to J/\psi\,\eta') = (Y.Y ^{+Y.Y}_{-Y.Y}) \times 10^{-5},$$

with theoretical uncertainties dominated by the $\eta'$ decay constant, mixing angle, and higher-order corrections to the hard-scattering kernels. This prediction offers a benchmark for forthcoming high-statistics analyses at the LHC (LHCb and ATLAS/CMS), where the larger $b\bar{b}$ production cross-section and improved photon/neutral-pion reconstruction capabilities are expected to enable a precision measurement of both channels. A confirmation of the predicted hierarchy between $\mathcal{B}(B_d^0 \to J/\psi\,\eta)$ and $\mathcal{B}(B_d^0 \to J/\psi\,\eta')$ would provide stringent constraints on the interplay between short-distance QCD dynamics and long-distance $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing, further validating the pQCD framework for color-suppressed $B$ meson decays involving pseudoscalar mesons with flavor-singlet admixtures.
